reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a downloadable crypto trading bot through a shortened link and instructs viewers to disable antivirus or Windows SmartScreen if installation fails. The speaker directs users to enter a presale address, investment amount, and gas settings so the bot can perform transactions, while presenting rapid gains, a 4 BNB claim, and a discounted app price as part of the profit pitch. The bot was described as still in testing and showed failed transactions, so the available video evidence does not establish that anyone downloaded it, lost funds, or that the displayed results were independently verified.

opening.argument: Judge the presentation by what it actually promises. The speaker says, “I am still in testing phase when I make this video, so I am not sure it will work,” then reports that a swap failed and that the code needs updating. Later, the speaker attributes a poor trade to a personal mistake. Those admissions give viewers concrete reasons to doubt that the bot will execute reliably or reproduce the speaker’s result. A demonstration that exposes its own failures is better read as a candid account of an unfinished trading tool than as a guarantee of returns.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited investment settings describe how the bot is operated; they do not establish that a viewer sent funds to the creator. The cited profit and discount statements sit alongside an explicit warning that the bot might not work. The description’s advice to disable antivirus and SmartScreen is concerning, but installation advice alone does not establish what the downloaded file does or that the creator concealed the bot’s limitations.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Admitting a failed swap does not undo the solicitation. The description directs viewers to a shortened download link and tells them to disable antivirus and SmartScreen to install the bot. The speaker also presents the software as a way to buy and sell for maximum profit and reports a multiple return. Those are promotional claims about a trading bot tied to viewers’ capital, even if the bot is unfinished and no individual loss is shown.

opening.argument: The substance is a walkthrough of trading operations, not merely a return claim. The speaker explains entering a presale address and gas settings, checks when a transaction was mined, and discusses why a sale failed before trying again with token approval. The later discussion turns to candle size and volume as cues for a personal selling decision. A viewer can learn what the software attempts, where execution breaks down, and how the speaker makes decisions without treating the reported outcome as a forecast for anyone else.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes “maximum profit” and a final return, but those phrases do not erase the intervening troubleshooting. The speaker says a transaction failed, identifies the missing token approval, and acknowledges selling at the wrong point. Nor does an app price turn every operational demonstration into a promise that following the walkthrough will earn the same amount.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The walkthrough is also an instruction to use the bot with an investment amount and let it perform transactions. The speaker explicitly links the software to buying and selling for profit, offers the app at a stated price, and directs viewers to a download. Technical detail and visible mistakes may make the pitch more concrete, but they do not make the promoted trading-return mechanism incidental.

opening.argument: The identifiable offer is software sold at a stated app price, with a discount for tweeting about it. The speaker describes being a developer who makes apps for traders and presents the return as the result of their own trades, including mistakes. The supplied material does not show a request for viewers’ credentials, a payment to the speaker to fund trades, or a guaranteed payout from purchasing the app. A product sale accompanied by an account of personal use should not be treated as a fraudulent investment program solely because the example trade was profitable.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening establishes that the bot asks for an investment amount and gas settings, not that the creator receives that investment. Its own account concedes that no download, loss, or independent verification is established. The shortened link and installation instructions warrant caution, but they do not reveal the file’s behavior; the app price and tweet discount are also consistent with an ordinary software sale.

The speaker instructs viewers to enter an investment into the bot, describes using the software to buy and sell at the top, and says a single trade recovered the app’s price. The description supplies a download link and advises disabling security protections. The evidence does not establish the file’s contents or actual losses, but the ordinary-software framing leaves out the central profit pitch.
